If you wanted a structured weekly plan with zero input beyond the initial quiz, PlateJoy worked. Answer questions once, get a plan. No conversation needed. For people who found that approach comforting, it was a solid product.
PlateJoy's 50-question quiz was state of the art in 2012. You answered once, the algorithm filtered its recipe database, and you got a personalized plan. The problem: "personalized" had a ceiling.

A fixed recipe database can only contain so many options. Filter for vegan + nut-free + low-FODMAP + quick meals and you might have 30 recipes left. Those 30 get repetitive fast. Users noticed. The quiz captured your preferences on day one but couldn't keep up as your tastes evolved or your pantry changed.
This is the structural problem with every quiz-based meal planner, not just PlateJoy.

The acquisition made everything worse. RVO Health likely acquired PlateJoy for its health and wellness assets, not to run a meal planning product. The founder eventually moved on. Development stopped. Support evaporated. The recipe database froze in time. It's the same pattern that killed

This page sticks to what independent sources have reported about PlateJoy's shutdown and its product while it was live, then explains what MacroRecipe does the same, what it does differently, and what it does not do. It is written by the team behind MacroRecipe, so read it with that in mind — the goal is to be useful even if you land on something else.

PlateJoy's recipes were folded into Wellos, a separate app from the same parent company, RVO Health. Whether that move preserved any individual user's saved plans is not something a former PlateJoy account holder can check today, because there is no working PlateJoy login to sign in from.

Some subscribers report pro-rated refunds were offered around the shutdown, per PlateJoy's own former support center as indexed by search engines. If you were charged after the closure and never saw a refund, your card issuer or PayPal is the practical next step — there is no PlateJoy support inbox left to write to.

The preference quiz behind PlateJoy drove a genuinely large recipe library, filtered to what each person actually said they liked and could eat — professional reviewers rated it well for ease of use while it was live.

It is fair to say PlateJoy solved the "what do I cook this week" problem well for a lot of people, for a long time — the complaints below are mostly about billing and about the last couple of years under new ownership, not about the core idea.

You still get a weekly menu built from a quiz-style profile — your food preferences, allergies, the ingredients you want to avoid, your kitchen equipment — made of real, complete dishes rather than a bare nutrient target.
Recipes open step by step when it is time to cook, and a batch cooking mode groups the week's prep into one session if you would rather cook once and eat several times.

PlateJoy planned meals around your stated food preferences, not around a calorie or macro target — its own former support content described no macro-goal adaptation feature. MacroRecipe starts from a goal (cut, maintenance, muscle gain) and adapts real recipes so the day lands near your estimated calorie and protein numbers, and says so honestly when a day falls short instead of pretending.

The grocery list carries an estimated cost in your own currency, adjusted for your country's price level. You set a weekly grocery budget, and the app tells you when a week's estimated cost runs over it — an estimate, not a receipt, but a number PlateJoy's plan-around-preferences model never gave you.
There is no barcode scanner, and no daily food log you have to keep up with. You set your food preferences and your goal once; the app rebuilds the menu around them, week after week.

It is not free. The preview of your first menu is free, after which it is a paid subscription, worth weighing against your own budget. PlateJoy was never free either: its last-known pricing was around $12.99 for one month, $69 for six months, or $99 for a year, after a 10-day trial.

The difference shows up at the bottom of the list: an estimated total cost, so you know roughly what the week will run before you are at the register.

A Better Meal collects your goals, dietary preferences, allergies, foods to avoid, and recipe preferences, then creates a personalized dinner plan. You can adjust, swap, and add meals, but the starting point is not a blank calendar.

For shopping, A Better Meal connects with nearly 50 grocery and delivery services. The app guides you through a retailer search experience item by item. You choose the products and check out yourself, so the relationship with the retailer stays yours.

A Better Meal can also import recipes from websites, social media, and photos. That is useful when you are rebuilding a routine from recipes you already trust. It does not mean that a Mealime library, favorites, or account data can be migrated automatically. That capability is being investigated separately.
There is no current PlateJoy product to compare feature by feature. The honest comparison is between what former PlateJoy or Mealime users were looking for and what A Better Meal offers now.

If you want personalized recommendations, A Better Meal starts with your preferences and builds the dinner plan from there. If you want the grocery list to be downstream of the plan, the list is generated from the plan rather than assembled as a separate task. If you want retailer flexibility, A Better Meal is independent of a single grocery chain and works across its current integration roster.

No migration capability is claimed here. A Better Meal can import recipes from websites, social media, and photos, but automatic migration of Mealime or PlateJoy libraries, favorites, or account data is not currently promised.

This is a textbook acquisition death. A bigger company buys a smaller product, strips it for parts, and abandons the original users.
After the acquisition, PlateJoy's worst reviews are almost entirely about billing. Users report being charged after cancellation with no way to reach anyone.
With development frozen after the acquisition, recipe quality stagnated. The database was finite. Filter for your specific dietary restrictions and you'd cycle through the same meals within weeks.
